title: After major cancer surgery
subtitle: ERAS care, chyle leak, pancreatic fistula grading

red_flags.text: Tachycardia, new atrial fibrillation, fever or rising inflammatory markers from day three: anastomotic or pancreatic leak until imaging says otherwise.
A small bleed from a drain or the gut after pancreatic surgery: a sentinel bleed that may precede a pseudoaneurysm rupture.
Milky drain fluid that increases once the patient eats: chyle leak.
Persistent vomiting and a distended abdomen beyond the expected ileus: delayed gastric emptying, obstruction or a collection.
Calf swelling, unexplained breathlessness or hypoxia: cancer surgery carries a high thrombosis risk.

do_now.text: Follow the ERAS pathway: early oral intake, early mobilisation, multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, PONV prophylaxis, and avoidance of fluid overload.
Remove the urinary catheter and nasogastric tube as early as the operation allows; do not leave tubes in by habit.
Pharmacological and mechanical thromboprophylaxis; consider extending pharmacological prophylaxis to 28 days after major abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery.
Sentinel bleed after pancreatic surgery: urgent CT angiography and interventional radiology, not observation.

assess.text: Daily review against the expected trajectory: pain, mobility, oral intake, bowel function, drain volume and character, and observations.
Grade complications consistently so they can be audited and discussed honestly.
Nutritional intake and the need for supplementary feeding when oral intake lags.

investigate.text: Drain fluid amylase after pancreatic resection, interpreted against the serum upper limit of normal and the day after surgery.
Drain fluid triglycerides when chyle is suspected.
CRP trend: a falling value supports safe discharge; a rising value after day three needs an explanation.
CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast for suspected leak or collection, with oral or rectal contrast where it helps.

resuscitate.text: Goal-directed fluid therapy, avoiding both hypovolaemia and the weight gain that worsens ileus and anastomotic oedema.

Chyle leak: dietary modification (low-fat, medium-chain triglyceride diet), and escalation to nil by mouth with parenteral nutrition for a high-output or persistent leak; a somatostatin analogue may be considered.
Clinically relevant pancreatic fistula: keep the drain in situ, treat infection, drain undrained collections percutaneously, and support nutrition.

definitive.text: Grade pancreatic fistula per ISGPS 2016. Biochemical leak: drain amylase above three times the serum upper limit of normal on or after day three without clinical impact; no longer called a fistula. Grade B: a change in management (prolonged drainage beyond three weeks, percutaneous or endoscopic drainage, angiography for bleeding, or infection without organ failure). Grade C: reoperation, organ failure or death.

Grade chyle leak per ISGPS 2017: drain or wound output of any volume on or after day three with triglycerides of 110 mg/dL (1.2 mmol/L) or more. Grade A needs no or dietary treatment only; grade B needs prolonged nutritional restriction, parenteral nutrition, drainage, a somatostatin analogue or readmission; grade C needs invasive in-hospital treatment or critical care, or results in death.
Post-pancreatectomy haemorrhage from a pseudoaneurysm: angiographic embolisation or stenting first-line in a patient stable enough, with laparotomy if that fails.
Anastomotic leak with sepsis: source control by percutaneous drainage or reoperation, decided by physiology and the extent of contamination.

escalate.text: Consultant surgeon for any suspected leak, sentinel bleed or return to theatre.
Interventional radiology for collections and bleeding after pancreatic and hepatobiliary surgery.
Dietitian early for chyle leak, pancreatic fistula or poor oral intake.
Critical care for organ dysfunction; do not let a grade C complication declare itself on the ward.

notes: A biochemical leak after pancreatectomy is not a complication. Grading consistently stops overtreatment of numbers and undertreatment of patients.
ERAS is a bundle; its benefit comes from adherence to many small elements together, not any single one.
Failure to rescue, not the complication rate, is what separates high-performing cancer units. Recognise early, escalate early.
